title: Global CO2 transport industry set to reach USD 211 billion by 2060
gist: Wood Mackenzie projects the global CO2 transport industry could reach USD 211 billion by 2060, moving 3 Gtpa of CO2 including 200 Mtpa across borders, with Asia Pacific taking about 60% of investment. Pipelines dominate spend, repurposing gas pipelines could halve costs, and policy gaps are the swing factor for cross-border CCUS.

themes.theme: Size and geography of CO2 transport investment

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie says the global CO2 transport industry could be worth USD 211 billion by 2060, enabling 3 Gtpa of CO2 transport of which 200 Mtpa crosses international borders, with transport increasingly determining CCUS project viability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sizes a midstream CCUS market for pipeline, shipping and engineering suppliers; the forecast is a long-dated model output.

insights.claim: Asia Pacific accounts for about 60% of CO2 transport investment due to long distances and large projected volumes, followed by North America and Europe, and over 80% of global transport investment goes to pipelines linking mostly onshore emitters to storage.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Capital for CCUS midstream skews toward Asia and pipe, shaping which contractors and regions benefit.

insights.claim: A mismatch between CO2 volumes and domestic storage availability is driving emergence of cross-border CO2 trade and liquefied CO2 (LCO2) shipping, particularly in Europe and Asia Pacific.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Creates a new shipping niche (LCO2 carriers) tied to storage-poor emitters.

insights.claim: Pipeline and shipping costs are comparable up to about 1,000 km, so the choice between them depends on factors like existing infrastructure; the lead analyst says geography sets the challenge while economics decides the mode.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Chiang
insights.so_what: Mode choice is site-specific, so uniform assumptions about CCUS transport cost can mislead.
insights.quote: Pipeline and shipping costs are comparable for distances up to 1,000 km

insights.claim: Repurposing existing gas pipelines could cut capital expenditure by over 60% and halve total CO2 transport costs, substantially improving pipeline economics versus shipping, though not all infrastructure can be repurposed and rigorous assessment is needed.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Owners of idle gas pipelines may gain CCUS optionality; asset suitability is the key diligence item.

insights.claim: Pipelines are capital-intensive with high fixed steel and construction costs that require high utilisation, whereas shipping costs are driven by operations, with fuel and electricity over 50% of levelized cost, giving ships greater flexibility for early-stage projects; pipelines become more economic as volumes scale.
insights.speaker: Bo Frohlich
insights.so_what: Early CCUS projects favor ships, mature hubs favor pipes; utilisation risk is the pipeline investor's exposure.
insights.quote: pipelines become more economic as volumes scale but shipping gives early-stage projects the flexibility needed to manage risk

insights.claim: Low-pressure CO2 vessels carry denser cargo in fewer, larger ships and can cut costs by up to 34% over long distances versus medium-pressure alternatives, a difference marginal on short European routes but decisive on typical Asia Pacific cross-border distances.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Favors low-pressure ship designs for Asian long-haul CO2 shipping.

themes.theme: Asia Pacific cross-border CCS and Japan

insights.claim: By 2060, cross-border CO2 transport demand from Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan is projected at 164 Mtpa against 187 Mtpa of storage capacity across Australia and Southeast Asia, with Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia as storage hotspots competing to serve the north.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Storage-rich Southeast Asian and Australian jurisdictions could earn CO2 import revenue; capacity is nearly fully used by projected demand.
insights.locator: Asia Pacific presents a compelling cross-border

insights.claim: Japan targets storing 120-240 Mtpa of CO2 by 2050 but has limited domestic storage; Wood Mackenzie estimates it may need to ship nearly 50 Mtpa across borders, close to its roughly 65 Mtpa of LNG imports, with shipping adding about USD 40/tCO2 or almost 30% of total levelised CCS cost.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Japan's CCS bill and shipping demand are large; CO2 logistics may mirror its LNG supply chain in scale.

insights.claim: In Japan's offshore economics, at 5 Mtpa shipping becomes more cost-effective than pipelines beyond 400 kilometres.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Provides a breakeven rule of thumb for planners and shipbuilders.
insights.locator: Offshore pipeline and shipping economics in Japan

insights.claim: Permitting delays, land acquisition problems and regulatory uncertainty raise pipeline costs, and gaps in cross-border bilateral agreements, liability frameworks and economic incentives limit cross-border CCS networks, especially in Asia where policy coordination could shape routes and project viability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cross-border CCUS timing depends on government treaties rather than technology; monitor bilateral deals and liability rules.
insights.quote: Policy and bilateral agreements will determine whether cross-border CCUS networks are realised
